title: Prefix Sum
summary: Precompute running totals once, and the sum of any range becomes a single subtraction — O(n) preprocessing buys O(1) range queries.

analogy.beginner: Kilometre markers on a highway. To find the distance between exit 12 and exit 47 you don't drive the road measuring as you go — you subtract the two marker numbers. Someone measured the distance from the start once, and now every 'how far between these two points?' question is one subtraction.
analogy.interview: Build P[i] = sum of the first i elements. Then sum(i..j) = P[j+1] - P[i] in O(1). This converts repeated range aggregation from O(n) per query to O(1) after O(n) preprocessing, and — combined with a hash map of previously seen prefix values — turns 'count subarrays with sum k' from O(n²) into O(n).

intuition:
Two ideas, and the second is the one that wins interviews.

**Idea one: range queries.** If `P[i]` holds the total of everything before index i, then the sum from i to j is `P[j+1] - P[i]`. The bigger total minus the smaller total leaves exactly the middle. Answer any range in one subtraction, forever.

**Idea two: subarray counting.** Rearranging that identity gives something much more powerful. If `sum(i..j) == k`, then `P[j+1] - P[i] == k`, so `P[i] == P[j+1] - k`. Read that right to left: *while scanning, at each position I know what earlier prefix value I need — so instead of searching for it, I look it up.*

That is the same move that turns Two Sum from O(n²) into O(n): a HashMap answers 'have I seen this value?' in O(1). Prefix Sum plus HashMap is one of the highest-yield combinations in the whole pattern catalogue, and it is the correct tool exactly where the sliding window breaks — arrays containing negative numbers.

bruteForce.whySlow: With n = 100,000 and q = 100,000 that is up to 10¹⁰ additions. Worse, the queries overlap heavily — the same stretches are re-added thousands of times.

problemFirst.observation: Every range sum is the difference of two totals-from-the-start. Those totals do not depend on the queries at all, so they can be computed once, before any query arrives.
problemFirst.leap: Precompute the running totals in one pass. Then each query is one subtraction: O(n) once, O(1) per query, and 10¹⁰ operations become 200,000.

howItWorks: **Build**: `prefix[0] = 0` and `prefix[i+1] = prefix[i] + nums[i]`. Use length n+1 — the leading zero removes every special case for ranges starting at 0.
**Query**: `sum(i..j) = prefix[j+1] - prefix[i]`, inclusive on both ends.

**Counting subarrays with sum k**: scan once keeping a running prefix; at each step look up how many earlier prefixes equalled `running - k`. Seed the map with `{0: 1}` — that entry represents the empty prefix and is what lets a subarray starting at index 0 be counted.
**2D prefix sums** answer rectangle queries with inclusion–exclusion: `S = P[r2][c2] - P[r1-1][c2] - P[r2][c1-1] + P[r1-1][c1-1]`.
**Difference array** is the inverse: to add v across many ranges, record `diff[i] += v; diff[j+1] -= v;` in O(1) per update, then take one prefix sum at the end to materialise the result.
**Other aggregates work too** — prefix XOR, prefix product (beware zeros), prefix counts of a character.

signals: Repeated range-sum or range-average queries over a static array
'Count the subarrays whose sum equals k' → prefix + HashMap
'Subarray sums divisible by k' → prefix remainder + HashMap
The array contains **negative numbers** and you need subarray sums — the sliding window is unsafe here
Many range *updates* with a single read at the end → difference array
antiSignals: The array changes between queries — a static prefix array goes stale on every write; use a Fenwick/segment tree for O(log n) updates
You need the maximum over a range, not the sum — max has no inverse, so subtraction does not work (use a sparse table or segment tree)
All values are positive and you need the longest/shortest range meeting a condition — a sliding window is simpler and O(1) space

complexity.time: O(n) preprocessing, O(1) per range query; O(n) total for the HashMap counting variant
complexity.space: O(n) for the prefix array or the map; O(1) if you only need a running total and no lookups
complexity.why: Building the prefix array is a single pass of one addition each. Each query is one subtraction regardless of range width — that is the whole point, and it is why the pattern beats a sliding window for repeated arbitrary queries. The counting variant is O(n) because each element contributes one map lookup and one map insert, both O(1) on average. Note the classic trade: the array must be static, because a single update invalidates every prefix from that index onwards — O(n) to repair. If updates interleave with queries, a Fenwick tree gives O(log n) for both.

commonMistakes.fix: With a leading zero and length n+1, the inclusive sum of i..j is `prefix[j+1] - prefix[i]`. Check it against a single element: sum(2..2) should be `prefix[3] - prefix[2]`.
Subarrays that start at index 0 are then missed entirely. The zero entry stands for the empty prefix.
Sums over large arrays exceed 2.1 billion easily. Use `long`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a sliding window on an array with negatives
commonMistakes.fix: Extending the window can decrease the sum, so shrinking on invalidity is unsound. Prefix + HashMap is the correct tool.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rebuilding the prefix array after every update
commonMistakes.fix: That is O(n) per update. Use a Fenwick (binary indexed) tree for O(log n) updates and queries.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to use prefix arrays for range maximum
commonMistakes.fix: Subtraction recovers a range only for invertible operations. Max is not invertible — use a sparse table or segment tree.

realWorldUses: Analytics dashboards: cumulative revenue by day, then any date range is one subtraction.
Image processing: the summed-area table is a 2D prefix sum, used for constant-time box blur and in the Viola–Jones face detector.
Databases maintain running aggregates for `SUM() OVER (ORDER BY …)` window functions.
Billing and metering systems store cumulative counters; usage for a period is the difference of two readings — exactly like an electricity meter.
Difference arrays power bulk range updates such as seat or inventory reservations.
interviewNotes: When you see 'subarray sum' plus 'negative numbers allowed', say 'prefix sum with a hash map' — it is the intended answer and the sliding window is the trap.
Mention the static-array caveat unprompted, and name the Fenwick tree as the answer when updates are interleaved. It is a strong signal.
The relationship between Two Sum and Subarray Sum Equals K is worth stating: both are 'I know what I need, so I look it up rather than search for it'.

quiz.question: With prefix[0] = 0 and prefix[i+1] = prefix[i] + nums[i], what is the inclusive sum of nums[2..5]?
quiz.explanation: prefix[6] covers indices 0..5 and prefix[2] covers 0..1; the difference leaves exactly 2..5.

quiz.question: Why is the map seeded with {0: 1} when counting subarrays that sum to k?
options: It represents the empty prefix, so a subarray starting at index 0 whose running sum equals k is counted
quiz.explanation: When running == k, we look up running - k == 0. Without the seed that lookup returns 0 and every subarray beginning at index 0 is silently missed.

quiz.question: 'Count subarrays summing to k, where the array may contain negative numbers.' Which pattern?
quiz.explanation: Negatives break the sliding window's monotonicity assumption. Prefix sums make no such assumption — the identity P[j+1] - P[i] = k holds regardless of sign.

quiz.question: Elements are updated between queries. Why is a plain prefix array a poor fit?
options: One update invalidates every prefix from that index onwards, costing O(n) to repair
Prefix sums only work on sorted arrays
It is fine — updates are O(1)
quiz.explanation: The structure assumes a static array. A Fenwick (binary indexed) tree supports both point updates and prefix queries in O(log n), which is the standard answer to this follow-up.
